title: The neuron: weighted sum plus a bend
summary: A neuron multiplies each input by a weight, adds the products (a dot product), adds a bias, and bends the result with an activation function such as ReLU. Before the bend, it splits its input space with a straight line.
llm_link: The feed-forward part of every transformer block is thousands of these neurons side by side, each reading the same token vector with its own weights. GPT-2 bends with GELU, a smooth cousin of ReLU.
key_ideas: Weighted sum: z = w · x + b. Each weight sets how loudly its input is heard; a negative weight makes that input argue against firing.
The bias does not depend on the input. It sets how easily the neuron fires, like the height of a bar the weighted sum must clear.
With two inputs, the points where z = 0 form a straight line. The weight vector points across it toward z > 0; changing b slides the line without turning it.
The activation bends z: ReLU(z) = max(0, z) keeps positives and zeroes negatives; the sigmoid 1 / (1 + e^(−z)) squeezes z into (0, 1).
Without the bend a neuron is a linear function, and stacks of linear functions stay linear.

quiz.q: Predict the result: a ReLU neuron has w = [0.5, −1], b = 1 and receives x = [1, 2]. What does it output?
quiz.explain: z = 0.5·1 + (−1)·2 + 1 = −0.5. ReLU replaces negative values with zero, so the output is 0.

quiz.q: In a two-input neuron, what does increasing the bias b do to the line z = 0?
options: Nothing; the bias only matters after the activation
quiz.explain: The line's direction is set by w alone. Changing b moves every point's z by the same amount, so the line shifts parallel to itself.

quiz.q: You want a large value of input x₂ to make the neuron less likely to fire. What should you do?
options: Use a sigmoid instead of ReLU
quiz.explain: A negative weight turns its input into an argument against: the bigger x₂ is, the more it lowers z.

quiz.q: Which values can a sigmoid output?
quiz.explain: 1 / (1 + e^(−z)) approaches 0 for very negative z and 1 for very positive z, but never reaches either: a dimmer that never goes fully off or fully on.

quiz.q: Inside one feed-forward layer of a transformer, how do the neurons relate to each other?
options: They all read the same token vector, each with its own weights and bias
Only one neuron is active per token
quiz.explain: Every neuron in the layer computes its own weighted sum of the same input vector, so the layer produces many different numbers from one token.

problems.title: One ReLU neuron
problems.prompt:
Write neuron(x, w, b) for plain Python lists: compute the weighted sum z = w·x + b, then return max(0, z) (ReLU).

If x and w have different lengths, raise a ValueError: a weight per input is the whole idea.

neuron([1, 2], [0.5, 1], 0)     # 2.5
neuron([1, 2], [0.5, -1], 1)    # 0   (z was -0.5)

tests.name: positive sum passes through
tests.code:
out = neuron([1, 2], [0.5, 1], 0)
assert abs(out - 2.5) < 1e-9, f'expected 2.5 (0.5*1 + 1*2 + 0), got {out}'

tests.name: negative sum becomes zero
tests.code:
out = neuron([1, 2], [0.5, -1], 1)
assert out == 0, f'z = 0.5 - 2 + 1 = -0.5, and ReLU turns negatives into 0, but you returned {out}'

tests.name: bias is added
tests.code:
out = neuron([0, 0], [3, 4], 1.5)
assert abs(out - 1.5) < 1e-9, f'with zero inputs the output should be just the bias 1.5, got {out}. Did you forget + b?'

tests.name: works for three inputs
tests.code:
out = neuron([0.8, 0.3, 0.5], [1.5, -2.0, 0.7], 0)
assert abs(out - 0.95) < 1e-9, f'expected 0.95 (the example from the video), got {out}'

tests.name: rejects mismatched lengths

hints: Check lengths first: if len(x) != len(w): raise ValueError("one weight per input")
The weighted sum is a dot product: z = sum(wi * xi for wi, xi in zip(w, x)) + b
ReLU is one call: return max(0, z)

problems.title: Swap the bend
problems.prompt:
Real networks use different activations, so pass the bend in as a function. Write:

  • relu(z): max(0, z)
  • sigmoid(z): 1 / (1 + e−z), using math.exp
  • neuron(x, w, b, activation): the weighted sum plus bias, passed through activation
neuron([1, 2], [0.5, -1], 1, relu)      # 0
neuron([1, 2], [0.5, -1], 1, sigmoid)   # 0.3775...  (sigmoid(-0.5))

Functions are values in Python: activation(z) calls whichever function was passed in.

tests.name: relu
tests.code: assert relu(3) == 3 and relu(-2) == 0, f'relu(3) should be 3 and relu(-2) should be 0, got {relu(3)} and {relu(-2)}'

tests.name: sigmoid(0) is one half
tests.code:
out = sigmoid(0)
assert out is not None and abs(out - 0.5) < 1e-9, f'sigmoid(0) = 1 / (1 + 1) = 0.5, got {out}'

tests.name: sigmoid stays between 0 and 1
tests.code:
hi, lo = sigmoid(10), sigmoid(-10)
assert 0.99 < hi < 1 and 0 < lo < 0.01, f'sigmoid(10) should be just below 1 and sigmoid(-10) just above 0, got {hi} and {lo}. Check the sign inside exp.'

tests.name: neuron uses the activation it is given
tests.code:
a = neuron([1, 2], [0.5, -1], 1, relu)
b = neuron([1, 2], [0.5, -1], 1, sigmoid)
assert a == 0, f'with relu the output should be 0, got {a}'
assert b is not None and abs(b - 0.37754) < 1e-4, f'with sigmoid the output should be sigmoid(-0.5) = 0.3775, got {b}'

hints: relu: return max(0, z). sigmoid: return 1 / (1 + math.exp(-z))
neuron: z = dot(w, x) + b, then return activation(z)

problems.title: Choose the weights: an AND gate
problems.prompt:
A neuron's line can separate the corner (1, 1) of the unit square from the other three corners. Pick numbers for w and b so that a sigmoid neuron outputs more than 0.5 only for x = [1, 1] and less than 0.5 for [0, 0], [0, 1] and [1, 0].

No training here: think about the line z = 0. Where must it pass so that (1, 1) is on the positive side and the other corners are not?

tests.name: fires for [1, 1]
tests.code:
out = neuron([1, 1], w, b)
assert out > 0.5, f'for [1, 1] the output should be above 0.5 but is {out:.3f}; z = w1 + w2 + b must be positive'

tests.name: silent for [0, 0]
tests.code:
out = neuron([0, 0], w, b)
assert out < 0.5, f'for [0, 0] the output should be below 0.5 but is {out:.3f}; here z is just b, so b must be negative'

tests.name: silent for one input alone
tests.code:
o1, o2 = neuron([1, 0], w, b), neuron([0, 1], w, b)
assert o1 < 0.5 and o2 < 0.5, f'[1, 0] gave {o1:.3f} and [0, 1] gave {o2:.3f}; each single weight plus b must stay negative'

hints: For [0, 0] the sum is just b, so b must be negative.
Each weight alone must not overcome b, but the two together must: w1 + b < 0, w2 + b < 0, w1 + w2 + b > 0.
One answer: w = [1, 1], b = -1.5. The line x1 + x2 = 1.5 cuts off the corner (1, 1).
